{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Vulvodynia (provoked vestibulodynia)", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Lichen sclerosus", "confidence": 0.88}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic candidiasis (recurrent or atypical)", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Vulvar lichen planus", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) grade 2–3", "confidence": 0.52}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.542, "reasoning": "The chronicity (1 year), severe pruritus, and progressive dyspareunia—especially with avoidance of intercourse—strongly suggest a neuropathic or inflammatory vulvar dermatosis. Provoked vestibulodynia is the most likely diagnosis given the hallmark features: localized entry pain (consistent with the tampon question, though unconfirmed), normal-appearing skin, and absence of infection signs; it commonly presents with long-standing itch-pain overlap due to central sensitization. Lichen sclerosus is highly plausible: it causes intense pruritus, introital dyspareunia, and can appear subtle early on—especially in postmenopausal or perimenopausal women—though classic findings (white plaques, architectural changes) may be absent initially. Chronic candidiasis remains in the top differential because atypical presentations (e.g., non-albicans species, biofilm-associated) can cause persistent pruritus and dyspareunia without overt erythema or discharge, and often evade standard testing. Vulvar lichen planus overlaps clinically with lichen sclerosus but more commonly features violaceous papules, erosions, or Wickham striae—and may coexist; its inclusion reflects the chronic inflammatory phenotype. VIN is lower-confidence (0.52) because while it can cause pruritus and pain, it typically presents with visible lesions (pigmented, raised, or ulcerated), and dyspareunia is less prominent than in neuropathic/inflammatory conditions—yet it must be ruled out given the duration and symptom burden, especially if exam reveals any mucosal abnormality."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Lichen sclerosus", "confidence": 0.95}, {"diagnosis": "Vulvovaginal atrophy (genitourinary syndrome of menopause)", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Lichen planus (vulvar erosive subtype)", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic vulvar candidiasis (refractory, non-acute)", "confidence": 0.45}, {"diagnosis": "Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) – differentiated type (associated with lichen sclerosus)", "confidence": 0.38}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.912, "reasoning": "The constellation—chronic vulvar pruritus (>1 year), dyspareunia progressing to avoidance, porcelain-white plaques, labial atrophy, clitoral hood retraction, and perianal wrinkling—is highly characteristic of lichen sclerosus (LS), which explains both inflammation-driven itch and scarring-induced stenosis/pain. The clinical findings (dry, thin, white plaques; atrophy; perianal involvement) are diagnostic hallmarks; biopsy remains gold standard but clinical diagnosis is often definitive in classic cases. Vulvovaginal atrophy is plausible given age-related estrogen loss causing thinning, dryness, and dyspareunia—but typically lacks porcelain-white plaques or perianal wrinkling, and pruritus is usually milder/more generalized; thus ranked second. Lichen planus may mimic LS but more commonly presents with violaceous papules, erosions, or Wickham striae—not classic crinkled white plaques—and perianal involvement is less symmetric; still plausible due to overlapping features and chronicity. Chronic candidiasis is unlikely: no mention of satellite lesions, erythema, or discharge; lesions are plaque-like and atrophic rather than inflammatory/macerated; and symptoms persist despite likely prior antifungal trials (implied by duration and severity). VIN (differentiated type) is a low-probability concern because it arises almost exclusively in the context of longstanding LS and may be clinically indistinguishable—but it is a premalignant condition, not a primary diagnosis, and lacks independent explanatory power for the full symptom complex without biopsy evidence of dysplasia."}
